q: Before Brunello made the town famous, Montalcino was known for a sweet white pressed from Moscato. What is that wine called?
exp: Moscadello was the commercial wine of the zone for centuries and was traded well beyond Tuscany. It survives as a curiosity in still, frizzante and late-harvest forms.

q: In Montepulciano the local Sangiovese clone must supply at least what proportion of a Vino Nobile?
exp: The balance may include Canaiolo, Mammolo and other permitted varieties, so a Nobile is more often a blend than a Brunello is. The clone is called Prugnolo Gentile here.

q: A Nobile Riserva is held longer than the standard bottling before release. How long in total?
exp: The standard wine needs two years and the Riserva a third, part of which must be spent in bottle. Both are shorter requirements than Brunello carries.

q: Antinori first sold a barrique-aged Sangiovese as a table wine rather than a Chianti from the 1971 vintage. Which wine was that?
exp: Small French oak and a blend outside the rulebook meant it could not be labelled Chianti Classico, so it went out as a vino da tavola. The white grapes left the blend with the 1975 vintage, which is also when Cabernet was written in.

q: Merlot on a vein of blue clay in Bolgheri, in a vineyard first planted by Tenuta dell'Ornellaia, produces which single-variety bottling?
exp: The clay holds water through a hot coastal summer, which is why Merlot behaves there as it does nowhere else in Tuscany. The vineyard is a matter of a few hectares.

q: Guado al Tasso and Ornellaia share a denomination built on Bordeaux varieties. Which two lead it in practice?
exp: The rulebook allows Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc each from nothing up to the whole blend, and caps Syrah and Sangiovese at half, so the first two lead by practice rather than by rule. Bolgheri Sassicaia was carved out as its own DOC in 2013 and sits outside this denomination.

q: Which denomination covers Sangiovese grown broadly across the Maremma, sitting below Morellino di Scansano in the hierarchy?
exp: It gathers up the wide coastal plain and its hinterland under one name, in reds, whites and roses. Morellino remains the tighter, hillier zone within that country.

q: Tignanello's sister wine from the same hillside leans on Cabernet Sauvignon rather than Sangiovese. Name it.
exp: The plot faces south and takes its name from the sun, and the wine inverts its neighbour's proportions. A small share of Sangiovese still keeps it recognisably Tuscan.

q: Before the dry version was ever bottled commercially, Montefalco's Sagrantino was made in which style?
exp: The grapes were laid out to dry and then fermented on their skins, and the sweet passito was the traditional Easter wine of the district; the dry bottling only appeared in the 1970s. Drying suits a grape whose tannin is otherwise ferocious.

q: Which Umbrian DOCG south of Perugia is a Sangiovese-led red released only as a Riserva?
exp: The plain Torgiano red stays at DOC; only the longer-aged wine was promoted. It is one of the few Italian DOCGs that exists at Riserva level alone.

q: DNA profiling matched Verdicchio to a variety long grown in the Veneto under another name. Which?
exp: Verdicchio, Trebbiano di Soave and Trebbiano di Lugana proved to be one variety under three regional names. It is unrelated to the far more widely planted Trebbiano Toscano.

q: Umbria's best-known white grows on tufa beneath a cathedral town and was historically made off-dry. Name the wine.
exp: The soft volcanic rock under the town was hollowed into cellars that held a steady cool temperature, which favoured wines with sugar left in them. Most Orvieto today is finished dry.

q: Which native white grape gives Umbrian blends more body and grip than Trebbiano manages?
exp: Grechetto has thicker skins and holds acidity better, so it stands up to lees work and even to oak. It is increasingly bottled on its own rather than used to prop up a blend.

q: Marche grows Verdicchio in a smaller inland valley that never opens to the sea. Name that zone.
exp: The valley runs north to south rather than out to the Adriatic, so it gets a continental swing of temperature the coastal Castelli di Jesi never sees. The wines are leaner and slower to open.

q: A Montepulciano-based red comes off a limestone headland rising straight out of the Adriatic near Ancona. Name the wine.
exp: Monte Conero is the only real promontory on that long flat coast, and its limestone gives a firmer wine than Montepulciano usually makes. Rosso Piceno, further south, blends the grape with Sangiovese instead.

q: A bishop's servant is said to have chalked his verdict on inn doors along the road to Rome near Lake Bolsena. Which wine took its name from that tale?
exp: The scout was sent ahead to mark where the wine was good, and doubled the word twice at Montefiascone. The story has outlived any reputation the wine itself holds.
